script.opening_words:
Two people, same city, same age, both
28, both just landed their first real
job. Both opened a brokerage account on
the same Tuesday afternoon in the same
October, depositing the same $300 a
month into the same S&P 500 index fund.
Now it's 30 years later. The first
person is sitting at a kitchen table
with a cup of coffee watching the number
in their account clear $600,000. They're
58. They haven't done anything
spectacular with their life financ
script.ending_words:
% contribution
increase on a specific date every year
without exception. That's it. The whole
thing.
Profoundly, aggressively, almost
offensively boring. No ticker to watch,
no moves to make, no moment of
cleverness.
Compounding doesn't care how smart you
are. It doesn't care about your salary,
your degree, your spreadsheets, or how
many finance podcasts you've queued up.
It cares about exactly one thing,
whether you left it alone long enough.
Um the people who end up with the
extraordinary late years aren't
financial geniuses, they're just the
people who were too boring to quit. Go
be boring.
script.analysis: All 18,469 stored characters read in two contiguous ranges with canonical hash match. Hook: two 28-year-olds investing $300/month; one stays 30 years (~$600K), one quits after a dip (~$41K). Compounding map ($10,000 at 10%: 10/20/30/40-year values; final decade 62% of gains, first decade 3.6%), Buffett wealth-after-50, exponential growth bias and lily-pad puzzle. 7: rule of 72 (Pacioli 1494), rolling S&P windows. 5: diversification across five asset roles with F1 pit-crew metaphor and drawdown-recovery math. 3: doubt, frustration, panic phases with 2008/2020 crash recoveries and Dalbar 2024 behavior gap. 1: annual 5% contribution increase ($300 -> 8% 30-year comparison), Schwab claim, Marcus vs Diane at $400/month for 33 years, Munger quote, action checklist (7-year date, five-category check or target-date fund, automation, written panic plan, scheduled increase), "Go be boring" close. Engaging structure with clear framework, humor and concrete tables; several worked examples in the second half do not reconcile. No sponsor/community CTA. ASR not audio-verified.

claim_audit: 0:9300 $10,000 at 10%: $25,937 / $67,275 / $174,494 / $452,593 at 10/20/30/40 years all correct; final-decade gain $278,099 = 62.8% and first-decade $15,937 = 3.6% of total gains, correct. $300/month for 30 years reaching ~$600K requires ~9.5% (10%: ~$678K; 9%: ~$549K). Buffett ~$1M at 30, billionaire at 56 and ~99% of wealth after 50 consistent with common accounts; "$300M at 50" approximate. Lily pad half-covered on day 47 correct. Rule of 72 traced to Pacioli's 1494 Summa, friend of Leonardo, correct.

0:9300 Rolling S&P windows: ~74% positive 1-year windows plausible; "over 95%" positive 7-year windows conflicts with the next sentence "every single seven-year rolling period ... positive" - both cannot hold, and historical 7-year windows ending in the 1930s and around 2008 were negative or near zero. A 60% drop needs +150% to recover, correct. ~10% nominal annual index return since 1926 consistent.

9300:18469 March 2020 -34% in 23 trading days, recovery by August 2020, and 2008 losses recovered by 2013 consistent with S&P price history. Dalbar 2024 investor 16.54% vs S&P 25.02% and 15th straight year consistent with Dalbar QAIB 2025 as publicized. $300/month at 8% for 30 years ~$408K matches annual compounding (~$447K monthly). 5% annual step-up: year-10 contribution is ~$465 (script $489 is year 11); ending ~$749K monthly-compounded vs script ~$787K - approximately "nearly double". "$15 becomes $379,000" misattributes the whole escalation gain to the first $15; $15/month at 8% for 30 years is ~$22K. Schwab "1% increase -> 25% more wealth after 20 years" unverified.

9300:18469 Marcus/Diane do not reconcile: $400/month with 5% annual increases at 8% for 33 years gives ~$1.34M with ~$384K contributed (script $1.1M, $430K contributed); at 42 ~$89K and 52 ~$343K (script $73K and $229K). Flat $400/month at 8% for 33 years gives ~$773K with $158,400 contributed; Diane's 11 months with half in cash cannot reduce that to $389K (implies ~4.7% average return). Munger "never interrupt it unnecessarily" quote is widely attributed. Target-date funds as automatic diversification correct.
